title: Definition and empirical existence of essential sparsity in large pre-trained transformers
content:
Essential sparsity is defined as a sparsity level at which a one-shot mask obtained by removing the smallest-magnitude weights from a pre-trained parameter vector $\theta_p$ yields downstream evaluation $\mathcal{E}^{\mathcal{T}}(f(x; m\odot\theta_p))$ within $\epsilon$ of the dense baseline $\mathcal{E}^{\mathcal{T}}(f(x;\theta_p))$, but any further small additional pruning $\mathcal{P}_\rho(m)$ causes the evaluation to fall below $\mathcal{E}^{\mathcal{T}}(f(x;\theta_p))-\epsilon$. Formally, if
      $$
      \mathcal{E}^{\mathcal{T}}(f(x; m\odot\theta_p)) \ge \mathcal{E}^{\mathcal{T}}(f(x;\theta_p)) - \epsilon
      $$
      and
      $$
      \mathcal{E}^{\mathcal{T}}(f(x; \mathcal{P}_\rho(m)\odot\theta_p)) < \mathcal{E}^{\mathcal{T}}(f(x;\theta_p)) - \epsilon,
      $$
      then the corresponding sparsity $1-\frac{\|m\|_0}{|m|}$ is an essential sparsity for model $f$ on task $\mathcal{T}$. In the experiments $\epsilon$ is set to $1\%$. Across multiple pre-trained vision and language transformers (BERT-base, OPT-125M/350M/1.3B, ViT-base/large, DINO-base and a case study on Vicuna-7B), experimentally observed essential-sparsity ranges allow removal of roughly $30\%$–$50\%$ of weights by one-shot magnitude pruning (OMP) without exceeding the $\epsilon=1\%$ performance drop on many downstream tasks; beyond that sharp turning point the performance degrades rapidly.

title: Essential sparsity holds for structured N:M sparsity patterns
content: The essential sparsity phenomenon, defined as the sparsity level at which further pruning a small fraction $\rho$ of the remaining nonzero weights causes the downstream evaluation $\mathcal{E}^{\mathcal{T}}(f(x; \mathcal{P}_\rho(m)\odot\theta_p))$ to drop below $\mathcal{E}^{\mathcal{T}}(f(x;\theta_p))-\epsilon$ with $\epsilon=1\%$, also appears when enforcing hardware-friendly N:M fine-grained structured sparsity (each contiguous group of $M$ weights has at most $N$ nonzeros). In experiments on the OPT-350M language model, using N:M masks derived from one-shot magnitude pruning on pre-trained weights and evaluated on the MNLI, QNLI, RTE, and SST-2 tasks, a substantial fraction of low-magnitude weights can be removed under N:M constraints with negligible downstream performance loss up to an essential sparsity boundary, indicating that essential sparsity generalizes beyond unstructured pruning to N:M structured patterns.

title: Essential sparsity exists in modern LLMs (Vicuna-7B) and can be extended by advanced one-shot methods
content: One-shot magnitude pruning (OMP), which removes the lowest-magnitude weights from the pre-trained parameter vector $\theta_p$ of the Vicuna-7B large language model (7 billion parameters) and evaluates zero-shot on the MMLU benchmark (covering Stem, Humanities, Social Science, and Others), exhibits the essential sparsity phenomenon: the evaluation metric $\mathcal{E}^{\mathcal{T}}(f(x; m\odot\theta_p))$ remains within $1\%$ of the dense baseline $\mathcal{E}^{\mathcal{T}}(f(x;\theta_p))$ for a sizable fraction of removed weights, until a sharp turning point beyond which performance degrades rapidly. Furthermore, the SparseGPT one-shot pruning algorithm, applied under the same zero-shot evaluation, shows similar trends and can push the usable sparsity beyond that achievable by OMP at higher computational cost, demonstrating that one-shot methods can scale to modern LLM checkpoints.

title: Within the essential-sparsity range, one-shot magnitude masks match Lottery Ticket masks in performance and have very high mask similarity
content: Within the essential-sparsity range (the sparsity level at which one-shot magnitude pruning yields downstream fine-tuning performance within $\epsilon=1\%$ of the dense baseline), masks produced by one-shot magnitude pruning (OMP) on pre-trained models BERT-base and ViT-base display nearly identical downstream fine-tuning performance to masks obtained by Lottery Ticket Hypothesis (LTH) iterative prune–retrain procedures, across multiple tasks (MNLI, QNLI, QQP, SST-2, RTE, SQuAD v1.1 for BERT; CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, Tiny-ImageNet for ViT). For sparsity levels $s\in\{10\%,20\%,30\%,40\%\}$, the binary masks from the two procedures exhibit high cosine similarity (above $96\%$ and often above $98\%$). Performance differences between OMP and LTH become significant only beyond the essential-sparsity regime, where LTH's task-specific retraining can preserve accuracy at higher sparsity.

title: Self-supervised pre-training yields stronger emergent sparsification than supervised pre-training in identical ViT architectures
content: When two vision-transformer checkpoints with identical architecture are compared—supervised ViT-base versus self-supervised DINO-base—the self-supervised DINO pre-training produces a weight distribution more concentrated near zero, leading to approximately $14.37\%$ more zero weights in the DINO checkpoint and improved robustness to one-shot low-magnitude removal; consequently, DINO exhibits better essential sparsity (larger free-removable fractions where downstream fine-tuning performance after pruning, on tasks CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and Tiny-ImageNet, remains within $\epsilon=1\%$ of the dense baseline) and higher tolerance to one-shot pruning across these downstream tasks.

title: Sharp turning behavior of essential sparsity is downstream-task dependent and not simply a function of model size
content: The sparsity–performance curve exhibits a sharp turning point (the essential-sparsity boundary, defined as the sparsity level beyond which further small pruning causes the downstream evaluation to drop below the dense baseline minus $1\%$) whose location depends strongly on downstream task complexity rather than monotonically on pre-trained model size. For example, BERT-base shows a turning point at approximately $60\%$ sparsity on the MNLI and QNLI tasks, whereas OPT-1.3B cannot be pruned beyond about $40\%$ on the RTE task without a sharp performance drop, demonstrating that larger parameter count does not guarantee a larger free-removable fraction.
